expectations.text: Names both the local code-review and the plugin code-review:code-review in qualified form, and picks one with a stated reason
expectations.evidence: response.md: "I'll run `code-review:code-review` (the plugin skill, not the local `code-review` command)" - both sides named, plugin in qualified form, pick stated. routing.md contains an explicit "Name collision - which `code-review`" table with three rows: `code-review:code-review` (plugin skill) marked "**chosen**", `code-review` (local skill) marked rejected with a reason, and `/review` (local command) rejected. A reason accompanies the pick: "the plugin-qualified one is the fuller implementation (explicit scope resolution, per-cell planning, dedup/rank/triage, coverage reporting including unreached cells)". Minor inaccuracy: response.md calls the local `code-review` a "command" when it is a local skill; routing.md classifies it correctly as "local skill", so the fork is named correctly overall.

expectations.text: The stated reason for the review pick cites a property that skill actually declares, rather than an invented distinction
expectations.evidence: The pick is justified on properties the plugin skill genuinely declares. routing.md quotes the description directly and accurately: "The skill's own description scopes it to 'a multi-axis code review over an explicitly named scope ... returns the triaged findings' and the scope here is named - this branch, against its merge base." The four properties cited as making it "the fuller implementation" - explicit scope resolution, per-cell planning, dedup/rank/triage, and coverage reporting including unreached cells - all appear verbatim in substance in the plugin skill's declared description ("resolves the scope argument, discovers review units, writes one plan row per review cell before dispatching anything, then deduplicates, ranks and triages what comes back, reporting per-unit coverage including the cells it never reached"). Crucially, this run did NOT fall into the known trap: it never claims the plugin is limited to heavyweight repo-wide sweeps, and instead correctly reads 'an explicitly named scope' as covering a branch diff. It also correctly verifies the plugin's declared negatives against the request ("the user is not asking to post the review to a PR, send it to a colleague, or file it into a tracker"), which is an accurate reading of the skill's stated non-uses.

expectations.text: Routes cleanup to code-simplifier:code-simplifier, giving the reason that it runs tests between edits and reverts breakage where the local skill only advises
expectations.evidence: response.md: "I'll run `code-simplifier:code-simplifier` ... It preserves behaviour and verifies that by running your tests between changes, reverting anything that breaks them." routing.md rejects the local alternative on exactly the advises-vs-verifies contrast: "`code-simplification` | local skill | rejected - guidance-flavoured; the plugin skill is the one whose deliverable is the edited code, with test-verified behaviour preservation and propose-don't-edit on untested units". Both halves of the required reason are present and both are properties the plugin agent actually declares.

expectations.text: In response.md specifically, the user is told that a fork existed and why this side was chosen - not only in routing.md
expectations.evidence: response.md discloses only that a choice was made, never that a fork existed or why this side won. The two parentheticals - "(the plugin skill, not the local `code-review` command)" and "(the plugin skill, not the local `code-simplify` command)" - name a road not taken but give the user no indication that these are competing candidates for the same job, and attach no reason for preferring one. Everything following each parenthetical describes what the chosen skill does; nothing says why the local alternative lost. A reader of response.md alone learns there is a naming precision being observed, not that they had two genuine options. The full collision analysis - the candidate tables, the 'fuller implementation' rationale, the advises-vs-verifies contrast - lives entirely in routing.md, which the expectation explicitly excludes. Contrast with the with_skill run, whose response.md opens "Both halves of that ask land on a name collision, so let me name the candidates in full before I pick either" and then gives the user both candidates and a reason for each pick.

execution_metrics.note: No transcript, metrics.json or user_notes.md exist for this run; response.md and routing.md are the entire artifact.

claims.claim: code-review:code-review is scoped to 'a multi-axis code review over an explicitly named scope ... returns the triaged findings'
claims.evidence: Quoted accurately from the plugin skill's declared description.

claims.claim: The plugin skill does explicit scope resolution, per-cell planning, dedup/rank/triage, and coverage reporting including unreached cells
claims.evidence: All four are declared: 'resolves the scope argument, discovers review units, writes one plan row per review cell before dispatching anything, then deduplicates, ranks and triages what comes back, reporting per-unit coverage including the cells it never reached'.

response.md calls it "the local `code-review` command". It is a local skill at /Users/peterkloss/.claude/skills/code-review/SKILL.md, not a command. routing.md classifies it correctly, so this is a slip confined to the user-facing reply - but it is the reply where the user would form their understanding of the fork.
`code-simplify` is indeed listed as a local command. Correct here.

claims.claim: The plugin skill gives findings across 'correctness, architecture, security and test coverage'
claims.evidence: response.md states this specific axis list. The plugin skill's description says 'multi-axis' and describes per-cell planning against 'the axis rubric', but does not enumerate these four axes - that list matches the LOCAL /review command's five-axis description ('correctness, readability, architecture, security, performance'). The run has attributed a neighbouring skill's axis list to the plugin. Not the trap named in the brief, and it did not drive the pick, but it is an unverified specific presented to the user as fact.

claims.claim: The bare name `code-simplifier` collides between the plugin skill and the plugin's same-named subagent
claims.evidence: Confirmed: the plugin ships agents/code-simplifier.md alongside the skill, both answering to `code-simplifier`.

claims.claim: Simplification would rewrite a diff that a human reviewer may already be reading
claims.evidence: A genuine and non-obvious consequence, raised in response.md with an offered alternative (merge first, clean up in a follow-up). No expectation covers it; it is the strongest content in this run's reply.

uncertainties: Executor asked the user to confirm which branch is in scope rather than assuming.

suggestions.expectation: In response.md specifically, the user is told that a fork existed and why this side was chosen - not only in routing.md
suggestions.reason: The wording bundles two separable requirements - that a fork existed, and why this side won. This run half-satisfies the first (it names an alternative without framing it as a competing option) and wholly misses the second. Splitting into two expectations would locate the defect more precisely and remove the judgement call about whether a bare parenthetical counts as 'telling the user a fork existed'.

suggestions.expectation: Names both the local code-review and the plugin code-review:code-review in qualified form, and picks one with a stated reason
suggestions.reason: Passes for any run that lists two names and attaches any sentence to the pick. Both arms passed it despite picking opposite sides on reasoning of very different quality. All the discrimination is in expectation 2.

No expectation checks the accuracy of what the run tells the user about the CHOSEN skill's capabilities. This run invented a specific four-axis list for the plugin that actually belongs to the local /review command - a fabricated capability claim in the user-facing reply that every expectation passes over. Expectation 2 only polices the reason for the pick, not the surrounding description.

No expectation covers the ordering rationale or the conditional handling of correctness findings, which both runs treated as substantive. This run also raised a real consideration no expectation rewards - that simplifying after review rewrites the diff a human reviewer may be mid-way through - and offered merging first as an alternative.

eval_feedback.overall: Expectations 2 and 4 discriminate well and correctly split this run from the other arm. Expectations 1 and 3 are close to free. The main gap is that nothing checks the factual accuracy of capability claims made about the chosen skill, as opposed to the rejected one.
